subject: wp
title: Accessible materials
prompt: Should accessibility checks be compulsory before course material is published? Write a 250-word argumentative essay.
modelAnswer:
Universities should require an accessibility check before course materials are published. Learning resources cannot fulfil their purpose when some students are unable to read or navigate them. A check would make inclusion part of preparation rather than an response after complaints.

First, accessible documents allow students to study independently. A structured text file can support searching, adjustable display settings and screen-reading software. By contrast, an image-only scan may contain the correct information while preventing effective use. Checking these features before distribution reduces avoidable barriers without changing the academic standard of the course.

Second, an organised process can save repeated remedial work. If every teacher receives a short checklist and an document template, problems can be identified early. The library or support team can then focus on difficult cases. This is more efficient than asking individual students to repeatedly explain the same obstacle after each upload.

Critics may argue that compulsory checking adds to an already demanding workload. That concern supports proportionate procedures and staff training, rather than leaving access to chance. A brief initial check can cover searchable text, useful headings and readable alternatives for essential images. Specialist help should remain available where a simple check is insufficient.

A requirement alone will not guarantee perfect access. Universities must collect feedback and correct problems that appear in use. Nevertheless, publication checks establish clear responsibility and reduce predictable failures. They recognise that a resource is ready only when students can use it to engage with the ideas it contains effectively and independently.

subject: wp
title: Loan delays
prompt: Investigate delayed returns in a laptop loan scheme and write a report for the library manager. For this simulated investigation, use these supplied notes: interviews with 18 borrowers and two library staff; observations during ten working days; six of 20 loans were returned late; 11 borrowers said they could not locate the return deadline; The confirmation message omitted the deadline. Include title, abstract/executive summary, introduction, methodology, findings, conclusion and recommendations. You may propose feasible actions. Do not invent additional results.
modelAnswer:
Investigation into Delayed Returns In A Laptop Loan Scheme

Executive Summary
This report examines delayed returns in a laptop loan scheme. Interviews and observations identified a service problem and a weakness in the arrangements supporting it. Clearer procedures and a short monitored trial are recommended. The evidence describes the investigation period and should not be treated as a permanent measure of performance.

Introduction
The investigation was requested by the library manager following concerns about delayed returns in a laptop loan scheme. Its purpose was to establish the main difficulties and propose practical improvements. The review covered routine use during ten working days; it did not attempt to assess every possible condition.

Methodology
The investigation combined interviews with 18 borrowers and two library staff and direct observations during ten working days. Interview responses were grouped by recurring concern. Observation notes were checked against these themes to distinguish reported experiences from events directly recorded. Participation was voluntary, and individual respondents were not identified. The limited sample restricts generalisation.

Findings
Six of 20 loans were returned late; 11 borrowers said they could not locate the return deadline. The confirmation message omitted the deadline. These observations identify both the immediate difficulty and a process requiring attention. They do not establish that every user had the same experience.

Conclusion
The evidence indicates that the current arrangements do not consistently meet users’ needs. The procedural weakness may contribute to the difficulty, although this brief investigation cannot establish its full effect. Improvement requires clear responsibility and follow-up rather than a single announcement.

Recommendations
The library manager should include a clear return date in every confirmation within two weeks. The same office should send a reminder one day before return is due during a four-week trial. At the end of the trial, the original observation procedure should be repeated and users invited to comment. Results should determine whether to retain or revise the changes.

subject: wp
title: Repair culture
prompt: Should workplaces prioritise safe repair over immediate equipment replacement? Write a 250-word argumentative essay.
modelAnswer:
Workplaces should prioritise safe repair before replacing equipment. This policy can reduce disposal and improve purchasing decisions, provided that safety and reliability remain conditions. Repair should be a reasoned assessment rather than a commitment to keep every old device indefinitely.

First, inspection prevents usable equipment from being discarded because of a minor fault. A damaged connector or replaceable component does not necessarily make an entire device worthless. Technicians can assess whether restoration is and test the result before returning it to service. This process gives the organisation a basis for choosing between repair and replacement.

Second, repair records reveal recurring weaknesses. If several devices fail in the same way, the purchasing team can consider durability and maintenance support when selecting equipment. Recording both the cost and success of repairs also prevents a vague environmental promise from concealing expensive or unreliable practices. Decisions become easier to review and explain.

Opponents reasonably worry that repairing equipment may interrupt work or create safety risks. Those risks justify clear limits. Unsafe devices should be withdrawn immediately, and replacements can support essential tasks during inspection. Where repeated repairs cost more than a replacement, the organisation should replace the item rather than defend repair at any price.

The strongest policy therefore combines technical judgement with records. Managers should assess service reliability alongside waste reduction and cost. Safe repair deserves priority because it treats replacement as a decision requiring evidence, while preserving the organisation's responsibility to provide equipment that staff can depend on throughout their working day.

subject: wp
title: Community participation
prompt: Should colleges recognise community volunteering as part of student development? Write a 250-word argumentative essay.
modelAnswer:
Colleges should recognise community volunteering as a part of student development. Participation can connect academic learning with responsibility, but recognition should respect community needs and students' circumstances. A voluntary, well-supported programme offers more value than a compulsory competition for service hours.

First, community work can develop skills that lectures alone cannot fully exercise. A student helping at a reading centre must listen, explain ideas clearly and adapt to different learners. These experiences create opportunities to practise patience and teamwork. Reflection afterwards can connect the activity with questions about communication, inclusion and responsible participation in shared institutions.

Second, a college can provide continuity that isolated volunteering often lacks. Staff can establish a partnership with a community organisation, train participants and agree on duties. This makes the programme more dependable for the host and gives students a clear understanding of their responsibilities. Community feedback should help determine whether the activity remains useful.

Critics may argue that recognition turns service into a credential and disadvantages students with limited free time. This concern is justified when institutions reward hours without considering circumstances. Colleges should therefore offer flexible opportunities and recognise participation rather than impose a universal quota. Students who cannot attend should retain access to other developmental activities.

Volunteering should also complement trained staff rather than replace necessary employment. With supervision, flexible participation and honest evaluation, colleges can support a meaningful relationship between learning and service. Recognition is worthwhile when it encourages responsibility and respects the people whom the programme is intended to support.

subject: wp
title: Garden maintenance
prompt: Investigate missed watering duties in a community garden and write a report for the community coordinator. For this simulated investigation, use these supplied notes: interviews with 12 volunteers and two caretakers; observations during two weeks; four scheduled watering sessions were missed; seven volunteers said duty changes were unclear; The shared rota had no procedure for confirming swaps. Include title, abstract/executive summary, introduction, methodology, findings, conclusion and recommendations. You may propose feasible actions. Do not invent additional results.
modelAnswer:
Investigation into Missed Watering Duties In A Community Garden

Executive Summary
This report examines missed watering duties in a community garden. Interviews and observations identified a service problem and a weakness in the arrangements supporting it. Clearer procedures and a short monitored trial are recommended. The evidence describes the investigation period and should not be treated as a permanent measure of performance.

Introduction
The investigation was requested by the community coordinator following concerns about missed watering duties in a community garden. Its purpose was to establish the main difficulties and propose practical improvements. The review covered routine use during two weeks; it did not attempt to assess every possible condition.

Methodology
The investigation combined interviews with 12 volunteers and two caretakers and direct observations during two weeks. Interview responses were grouped by recurring concern. Observation notes were checked against these themes to distinguish reported experiences from events directly recorded. Participation was voluntary, and individual respondents were not identified. The limited sample restricts generalisation.

Findings
Four scheduled watering sessions were missed; seven volunteers said duty changes were unclear. The shared rota had no procedure for confirming swaps. These observations identify both the immediate difficulty and a process requiring attention. They do not establish that every user had the same experience.

Conclusion
The evidence indicates that the current arrangements do not consistently meet users’ needs. The procedural weakness may contribute to the difficulty, although this brief investigation cannot establish its full effect. Improvement requires clear responsibility and follow-up rather than a single announcement.

Recommendations
The community coordinator should require duty swaps to be acknowledged by both volunteers within two weeks. The same office should review missed sessions after a four-week trial during a four-week trial. At the end of the trial, the original observation procedure should be repeated and users invited to comment. Results should determine whether to retain or revise the changes.
